title: What was the purpose of USAID?
summary: Hosts examine USAID (U.S. Agency for International Development) on the day it was absorbed into the State Department, after its final day as an independent agency on June 30. They cover its origins under John F. Kennedy in 1961 and precursors like the Marshall Plan, its Cold War soft-power purpose, notable successes (Green Revolution, smallpox eradication, PEPFAR, tuberculosis and malaria work), controversies (Afghanistan aid diversion, the Chemonics contract, the Alan Gross case in Cuba, the Kenya Children of God Relief Institute abuse case, the Gaza condoms claim), budget figures, a Lancet estimate of lives saved and deaths projected from cuts, and the debate over whether it was a good investment and what its loss means for democracy and China's influence. A listener mail segment at the end includes a correction about American Graffiti and Modesto, California.

entities.name: President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief

segments.title: Opening: USAID's final day and absorption into State Department
segments.summary: Hosts note June 30 was USAID's last day as an independent agency, with functions moving to the State Department; they recount reactions including Bono, George W. Bush and Obama, and Josh shares his view that the agency needed restructuring rather than abrupt shutdown. Marco Rubio's announcement of an 'America First' foreign aid agency is mentioned.

segments.title: What foreign aid is and how much it costs
segments.summary: The hosts break down US foreign assistance into humanitarian aid (about 25%), development (about 60%) and security funding (about 15%), describe the security aid to police and militaries, and note foreign aid is about 1% of federal spending with USAID at about 0.5%.

segments.title: Origins: Cold War soft power and the Marshall Plan
segments.summary: USAID was created in 1961 under Kennedy to build soft power against Soviet and Chinese influence, following containment policy. Its roots trace to the 1947 Marshall Plan, and MIT economists Walt Rostow and Max Millikan later argued for such aid as ongoing policy.

segments.title: Kennedy's influences: congressional trip, The Ugly American, and five-year budgets
segments.summary: Kennedy's 1951 congressional trip to Asia and the book The Ugly American shifted his views toward foreign aid. Kennedy pushed for five-year budgets for USAID, which Congress did not grant, leaving funding tied to annual budgets.

segments.title: Early successes: Green Revolution
segments.summary: More than half of 1960s USAID funding went to the Green Revolution led by Norman Borlaug, modernizing agriculture through irrigation, fertilization and crop rotation. Estimates credit it with saving about a quarter billion lives, contrasted with Mao's Great Leap Forward famine.

segments.title: Health successes: smallpox, PEPFAR, tuberculosis and malaria
segments.summary: Hosts describe USAID's partnership with the CDC to eradicate smallpox, the PEPFAR AIDS initiative launched in 2003, and estimated lives saved from tuberculosis work and the President's Malaria Initiative. They note the American flag branding on aid.

segments.title: Controversies: devil's bargains and Afghanistan
segments.summary: USAID aid was sometimes used as a negotiating chip during Cold War alliances. In Afghanistan, over $100 billion in aid reportedly saw about 40% go to officials, warlords, drug lords and insurgents, and counter-opium funding coincided with a sharp rise in opium cultivation in Kandahar Province.

segments.title: Chemonics contract and Alan Gross case in Cuba
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the $9.5 billion Chemonics medical supply contract, which was poorly managed with false reporting, and the case of Alan Gross, a USAID subcontractor arrested in Cuba in 2009 while setting up internet access, later exchanged for three Cuban prisoners.

segments.title: Handling misconduct: Kenya orphanage case
segments.summary: Hosts argue how an agency responds to wrongdoing matters. In Kenya, a whistleblower reported abuse at the Children of God Relief Institute, an orphanage funded by USAID; the USAID Inspector General found it knew or should have known, and USAID cut funding in 2023 and shared findings with Kenyan police.

segments.title: Gaza condoms claim
segments.summary: The hosts address the widely repeated claim that $50 million was spent on condoms in Gaza. They say the funding was $100 million to International Medical Corps in two tranches, mostly for emergency medical services, and its director said no dollar had yet been spent on condoms.

segments.title: Lancet estimate, budget figures, and whether it is a good investment
segments.summary: A Lancet study estimates about 91 million deaths prevented since about 2000 by USAID, with about 14 million more projected preventable deaths by 2030 due to cuts. Budget data show $21.7 billion in 2024, and USAID spending rose 106% since 1980 versus nearly 200% for total government. Hosts discuss the difficulty of calculating return on investment in goodwill and leverage.

segments.title: Public opinion, perception of aid spending, and global consequences
segments.summary: A 2019 Pew poll split opinion on foreign aid spending. Americans overestimate foreign aid at about a quarter of the budget versus roughly 1%. Hosts discuss USAID support for pro-democracy groups, and that its withdrawal may open a vacuum China could fill, with the US spending $3.8 trillion since WWII versus China's $1 trillion in about 12 years.

segments.title: Balancing the view and closing thoughts
segments.summary: Hosts say they tried to cover both sides, note critics of American influence may favor the cuts, and encourage listeners to make up their own minds.

segments.title: Listener correction: American Graffiti and Modesto
segments.summary: A listener corrects the hosts, saying American Graffiti is based on cruising culture in Modesto, California, where George Lucas grew up, not on the Sunset Boulevard cruising zone. The hosts respond, mentioning the band Grandaddy.

segments.title: Mail request and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh asks the listener to reply with clarification on whether he is a current Modesto resident and invites other email to the show address.
